concept: Parkinson's disease diagnosis and biomarkers: clinical criteria, prodromal stage, staging, genetics, alpha-synuclein seed amplification, imaging, epidemiology and rating scales
summary: Source-anchored research for Parkinson's disease diagnosis and biomarkers: clinical criteria, prodromal stage, staging, genetics, alpha-synuclein seed amplification, imaging, epidemiology and rating scales. Run status: COMPLETED.

facts.text: Neuromelanin-sensitive MRI is an emerging candidate biomarker, but the strong performance of a small retrospective 7T study does not establish its accuracy in premotor, equivocal or atypical cases: its authors explicitly called for studies in those populations. (low confidence)

MDS-UPDRS assesses four domains: Part I non-motor experiences of daily living, Part II motor experiences of daily living, Part III motor examination, and Part IV motor complications; it is used in clinical care and research. (medium confidence)

The original MDS-UPDRS clinimetric study tested 877 patients at 39 sites and found internal consistency of 0.79–0.93 across parts; factor analyses supported separate part sum scores in preference to an all-parts total. (low confidence)
An independent Spanish-language validation in 435 patients reported intraclass correlation above 0.85 for each part total, while noting a moderate floor effect (30 %) for Part IV. (low confidence)

Part III examination instructions require recording medication status, time since the last levodopa dose, and clinical ON/OFF state; these conditions matter when interpreting repeated motor examinations. (medium confidence)

In a study of the MDS-UPDRS Motor Examination (Part III) with 728 paired investigations of 260 patients, minimal clinically important difference estimates were asymmetric: −3.25 points for minimal clinically pertinent improvement and +4.63 for worsening, using clinician global-impression anchors and distribution methods. (low confidence)

A 2017 study of paired investigations from 365 patients estimated minimal meaningful changes in Part I of more than 2.64 points improvement or 2.45 worsening, and Part II of 3.05 improvement or 2.51 deterioration; these are study estimates for the specified parts. (low confidence)

Original UPDRS and MDS-UPDRS scores should not be treated as interchangeable: a 2012 calibration study supported conversion formulas for Parts II and III, but did not achieve concordance for Parts I and IV. (low confidence)

The MDS Non-Motor Rating Scale (MDS-NMS) consists of 13 domains plus a subscale for non-motor fluctuations and is rater-administered; in its initial multicenter validation study, internal consistency was acceptable (average Cronbach's alpha 0.66 and 0.84 for the scale total and the non-motor fluctuations total), interrater reliability was excellent (intraclass correlation coefficient >0.95) and test-retest intraclass correlation was 0.84 for the scale total. (low confidence)
SynNeurGe links its biological components to a clinical component C, defined by either a single high-specificity feature or multiple lower-specificity clinical features. (low confidence)

A critical review concluded that epidemiology alone makes causal attribution difficult because relevant exposures may precede manifest PD by decades; complementary experimental evidence increases causal plausibility. Observational associations should retain this qualification. (low confidence)

Pathogenic SNCA variants cause rare autosomal dominant PD; point mutations and gene multiplications are relevant variant classes. SNCA penetrance and phenotype depend on the variant. (medium confidence)

Conventional structural MRI identifies vascular damage, masses and patterns of atrophy that can cause or help distinguish parkinsonism; ordinary anatomical sequences have limited ability to identify the dopaminergic deficit itself. (medium confidence)
The 2015 MDS criteria first require motor parkinsonism: bradykinesia together with rest tremor, rigidity, or both. Parkinsonism alone does not establish PD as its cause. (medium confidence)

NICE NG71 recommends prompt, untreated referral to a specialist in differential diagnosis when PD is suspected, and regular diagnostic review at six- to twelve-month intervals with reconsideration if atypical features develop. Its diagnostic recommendation explicitly names the UK Brain Bank criteria. (low confidence)

A blinded comparison of three independent laboratories using PPMI CSF samples reported sensitivities of 86–96% and specificities of 93–100%, demonstrating reproducibility in expert laboratories despite methodological differences. (low confidence)

The 2025 biomatrix meta-analysis reported pooled blood SAA sensitivity of 0.90 (95% CI 0.86–0.93) and specificity of 0.91 (0.86–0.95); these pooled estimates are limited by aggregate data, publication bias and heterogeneous studies, and do not establish a universal blood-test performance. (low confidence)

In an analysis of PPMI and Tübingen cohort data, baseline SAA time-to-threshold predicted cognitive decline in both PPMI (hazard ratio 2·36, 95% CI 1·60–3·46) and Tübingen (2·17, 1·07–4·41), and was associated with cognitive decline in an Alzheimer-biomarker-negative PPMI subgroup. This was an observational prognostic association. (low confidence)

A 2025 modelling study using GBD 2021 projected 25.2 million people with PD worldwide in 2050 (95% uncertainty interval 21.7–30.1 million), a 112% increase from 2021; these are forecasts, not observed future counts. (low confidence) (verified as of 2025-03-05)

The paraquat evidence has conflicting interpretations: Tanner and colleagues’ 2011 Agricultural Health Study nested case-control analysis reported an association with PD (OR 2.5, 95% CI 1.4–4.7); EPA’s page updated November 3, 2026 states that it has not found a clear link between labeled paraquat uses and PD. The regulatory statement is qualified by labeled-use conditions. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-03)

A paraquat systematic review and meta-analysis (databases searched up to May 2019) found, across nine case-control studies, that PD occurrence was 25% higher in participants exposed to paraquat, while the only cohort investigation included showed a non-significant OR of 1.08; the authors concluded that the data indicate a positive association but that the weight-of-evidence does not enable one to assume an indisputable cause-effect relationship. (low confidence)

Tanner et al. reported an association between paraquat use and PD in FAME (110 cases, 358 controls; OR 2.5, 95% CI 1.4–4.7), whereas the later AHS prospective analysis reported no statistically clear association (HR 1.09, 95% CI 0.84–1.41). These overlapping study populations and different designs should not be counted as independent replications. (low confidence)

In the 2014 swallow-tail MRI study, retrospective-cohort diagnostic accuracy was 96% on diagnostic scans and fell to 91% when non-diagnostic scans were included; scan quality therefore materially affected the reported performance. (low confidence)

A 2024 retrospective 7T neuromelanin MRI study included 21 PD patients, 13 essential-tremor patients and 18 controls; substantia nigra pars compacta total volume distinguished PD from the pooled non-PD group with reported sensitivity 100% and specificity 96.8%. These are within-study results. (low confidence)

In the 2018 eight-centre validation cohort of 626 patients, probable MDS PD had 94.5% sensitivity, 88.5% specificity and 92.6% overall accuracy against expert clinical diagnosis. These estimates measure agreement with expert clinical diagnosis, not autopsy confirmation. (low confidence)

A 2024 Mayo Clinic retrospective study matched 186 women and 186 men with iRBD; 48 patients (12.9%) phenoconverted during median follow-up of 6.0 years. Only age at diagnosis remained associated with conversion in the adjusted model (HR 1.09, 95% CI 1.06–1.13); the unadjusted association with antidepressant use must not be interpreted as evidence of neuroprotection. (low confidence)

NfL interpretation needs covariate adjustment: the head-to-head study found associations with age in both CSF and plasma, and with body mass index, estimated glomerular filtration rate and chronic kidney disease in plasma. (low confidence)

The FDA’s August 19, 2024 Letter of Support recommends CSF SAA as a susceptibility/risk biomarker for trial enrichment and supports binary SAA assessment for selection into trials targeting common synuclein biology; its stated context is drug development and clinical trials. (low confidence) (verified as of 2024-08-19)

A Viewpoint cautions against premature adoption of the alpha-synuclein seed amplification assay as a Parkinson disease biomarker test in general neurology practice; this is an attributed clinical-implementation caution. (low confidence)

Neurofilament light chain can be measured in CSF and plasma as a marker of axonal damage; higher levels have been associated with poorer cognitive outcomes in Parkinson disease, but it is nonspecific and also rises with age and other inflammatory or degenerative conditions. (low confidence)

A 2019 PPMI analysis of 423 de novo patients estimated within-subject reliability of one-year change scores: Part II and Part III OFF each reached 0.50. Its authors cautioned that change scores contained substantial error variance. (low confidence)

Early-disease sensitivity requires caution: a Rasch analysis found floor effects and disordered response thresholds in Parts II and III; a separate comparison did not support greater sensitivity of MDS-UPDRS than UPDRS for mild motor severity in de novo PD. (medium confidence)

The MDS website describes the MDS-UPDRS as a revision of the original Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (developed in the 1980s) that addresses problematic areas of the original scale identified by an MDS review task force; it was developed to evaluate non-motor and motor experiences of daily living and motor complications, includes a motor evaluation, and can be used in clinical settings and in research. (low confidence)

The PDQ-39 is a short 39-item quality-of-life questionnaire for Parkinson's disease whose data can be presented in profile form or as a single index; a briefer derived measure (PDQ-8) also exists. (low confidence)

The Camp Lejeune result cannot uniquely attribute the association to TCE: exposure was inferred from residence, diagnostic data were limited to VHA/Medicare users, and PCE, vinyl chloride, benzene or mixtures could have contributed. (low confidence)

Air-pollution findings differ across settings: a Taiwan nationwide study reported positive associations for several pollutants that persisted in multipollutant models, while a Northern Ireland study found no overall association for medium-term PM₂.₅ or NO2 exposure and medication-defined PD onset; its under-50 subgroup showed a PM₂.₅ association. These exposure windows and outcome definitions limit direct comparison. (low confidence)

The same Global Burden of Disease analysis reported male-to-female ratios of age-standardised prevalence rates of 1·40 (95% UI 1·36-1·43) in 2016 and 1·37 (1·34-1·40) in 1990, and estimated 211 296 deaths (95% UI 167 771-265 160) due to Parkinson's disease in 2016. (low confidence)

The Global Burden of Disease investigators concluded that the global burden of Parkinson's disease more than doubled over the past generation as a result of increasing numbers of older people, with potential contributions from longer disease duration and environmental factors. (low confidence)

A 2023 narrative review in J Parkinsons Dis (Dorsey and colleagues) reports that trichloroethylene (TCE) was first linked to parkinsonism in 1969, that four case studies involving eight individuals have linked occupational exposure to TCE to PD, and that a small epidemiological study associated occupational or hobby exposure with a 500% increased risk; the authors postulate that TCE contributes to the global rise of PD and state that further research is necessary to examine this hypothesis. (low confidence)
Pathogenic LRRK2 variants cause autosomal dominant PD with reduced, age-dependent penetrance; inheriting a pathogenic variant does not guarantee disease. (medium confidence)

Marder and colleagues (2015) estimated PD risk to age 80 at 0.26 (95% CI 0.18–0.36) in relatives predicted to carry LRRK2 G2019S in an Ashkenazi Jewish kin-cohort. This is an ancestry- and ascertainment-specific estimate, not universal penetrance for every LRRK2 variant. (low confidence)

PRKN- and PINK1-related PD have autosomal recessive inheritance and are especially relevant in early-onset disease; established recessive disease must be distinguished from finding a single heterozygous variant. (medium confidence)

GeneReviews describes PRKN-related PD as usually beginning before age 35 with slow progression and relatively milder non-motor manifestations; PINK1-related PD has a similar phenotype, with psychiatric features more prominent. (low confidence)

Large studies have not demonstrated increased PD risk from a single heterozygous pathogenic PRKN variant. The UK Biobank/NIH-PD study found similar PD likelihood in single-variant carriers and noncarriers; this does not establish recessive PRKN disease in a monoallelic carrier. (medium confidence)

In the 2024 PD GENEration publication, 8301 participants had received results from enrollment through June 2023; 13% had reportable variants and 9.1% of those without the specified high-risk factors had reportable variants. Reportable included pathogenic, likely pathogenic and risk variants, so the yield is not a count of confirmed monogenic diagnoses. (low confidence)

GBA1 encodes the lysosomal enzyme glucocerebrosidase. Biallelic disease-causing variants are associated with Gaucher disease, whereas heterozygous variants can increase PD risk; these are different genetic counseling contexts. (low confidence)

GeneReviews explicitly describes disagreement about classifying GBA1-associated PD as monogenic disease or a risk-factor association, while noting that some Gaucher-causing variants have higher penetrance. The classification should be qualified by variant and population. (low confidence)
Heterozygous GBA1 variants increase PD risk with variable penetrance, whereas biallelic Gaucher-disease-causing GBA1 variants are associated with Gaucher disease. (medium confidence)

GBA1-associated PD risk depends on variant severity and genetic background; the UK Biobank/LuxPark study found that polygenic risk modified risk among carriers, so a single penetrance estimate should not be applied to every carrier. (medium confidence)

A meta-analysis of 17 datasets from Parkinson's disease genome-wide association studies in European ancestry samples identified 90 independent genome-wide significant risk signals across 78 genomic regions; these 90 variants explained 16-36% of the heritable risk of Parkinson's disease depending on prevalence. (low confidence)

Presynaptic dopamine-transporter imaging supports distinguishing essential tremor from neurodegenerative parkinsonism; an abnormal DaTscan is not specific for idiopathic Parkinson’s disease and cannot reliably separate it from atypical degenerative parkinsonism. (medium confidence)

Conventional structural MRI generally does not confirm PD, but can identify alternative structural causes or findings suggesting atypical parkinsonism; its sensitivity for atypical syndromes is limited early in disease. (medium confidence)

FDG-PET measures regional cerebral glucose metabolism and can support differentiating parkinsonian syndromes using disease-associated patterns; this is a different biological readout from presynaptic dopamine-terminal imaging. (medium confidence)

The EANM/SNMMI guideline describes fluorodopa PET as a presynaptic dopaminergic assessment and notes that atypical parkinsonian syndromes usually cannot be separated from idiopathic PD with this technique; FDG-PET instead evaluates metabolic patterns. PET tracers should therefore not be treated as interchangeable tests. (medium confidence)

PET measures depend on the tracer: fluorodopa uptake reflects tracer influx and decarboxylation in presynaptic dopamine assessment, whereas FDG-PET maps regional glucose metabolism and disease-related metabolic patterns. (medium confidence)

The EANM/SNMMI guideline warns that DAT binding reaches a floor later in disease, weakening its correlation with further clinical progression; scan signal should not be treated as a universally linear progression measure. (low confidence)

The DATSCAN label (revised 11/2022) states that its effectiveness as a screening or confirmatory test, and for monitoring disease progression or response to therapy, has not been established. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27)

In the DATSCAN label's two multicenter studies of 284 adult patients with suspected parkinsonian syndromes, the clinical reference category parkinsonian syndromes (PS) comprised Parkinson's disease, multiple system atrophy and progressive supranuclear palsy, and the label states that DATSCAN imaging was not designed to distinguish among these conditions. (low confidence)

NICE guideline NG71 (published 19 July 2017) recommends considering 123I‑FP‑CIT SPECT for people with tremor if essential tremor cannot be clinically differentiated from parkinsonism, and says not to use PET in the differential diagnosis of parkinsonian syndromes except in the context of clinical trials. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27)

NICE guideline NG71 (published 19 July 2017) says not to use structural MRI to diagnose Parkinson's disease, while structural MRI may be considered in the differential diagnosis of other parkinsonian syndromes. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27)

MDS red flags have explicit timing and severity: wheelchair-requiring gait progression within five years, severe autonomic failure within five years, and recurrent balance-related falls within three years; bilateral symmetric onset is another red flag. Confounding explanations and timing must be considered. (low confidence)

The 2015 MDS criteria were designed to codify expert clinical diagnosis for research and can guide clinical assessment; diagnostic accuracy varies with disease duration and examiner expertise, so criteria performance should not be treated as one universal accuracy number. (medium confidence)

A predominantly lower-limb gait syndrome can suggest vascular parkinsonism, but cerebrovascular imaging abnormalities are not conclusive because vascular disease and PD may coexist. Normal-pressure hydrocephalus is another potentially treatable mimic with gait, urinary and cognitive symptoms and ventriculomegaly. (low confidence)

The UK Parkinson’s Disease Society Brain Bank criteria, reproduced from Gibb and Lees (1988), first define a parkinsonian syndrome as bradykinesia plus at least one of muscular rigidity, 4–6 Hz rest tremor, or postural instability not caused by primary visual, vestibular, cerebellar or proprioceptive dysfunction (step 1); step 2 lists exclusion criteria for Parkinson’s disease, including supranuclear gaze palsy, cerebellar signs, early severe autonomic involvement and neuroleptic treatment at onset of symptoms. (low confidence)

Step 3 of the UK Parkinson’s Disease Society Brain Bank criteria lists supportive prospective positive criteria, three or more of which are required for diagnosis of definite Parkinson’s disease: unilateral onset, rest tremor present, progressive disorder, persistent asymmetry affecting the side of onset most, excellent response (70–100%) to levodopa, severe levodopa-induced chorea, levodopa response for 5 years or more, and a clinical course of 10 years or more. (low confidence)

The Movement Disorder Society task-force critique describes Hoehn–Yahr as nonlinear and heavily weighted toward postural instability, with incomplete coverage of other motor disability and no information on nonmotor problems. (low confidence)

In its report, the Movement Disorder Society task force recommended the original Hoehn–Yahr form for demographic group descriptions, reporting medians and ranges, and nonparametric analysis of changes; it reported no clinimetric data then available for the widely adopted half-stage modification. (low confidence)

Braak’s proposed pattern does not apply to every patient: the 2017 review limits its staging fit to a subset with young onset and long disease duration, while the 2008 critical evaluation reports exceptions and neurologically intact people with extensive postmortem pathology. (medium confidence)

Höglinger and Lang explicitly distinguish SynNeurGe classification from staging: they refrained from proposing disease stages pending prospective evidence establishing temporal order; NSD-ISS is a separate staging proposal. (low confidence)

In their 2024 comparison, Höglinger and Lang classify an isolated S-positive result without confirmed neurodegeneration as Parkinson’s/Lewy-type synucleinopathy, whereas they describe NSD-ISS as assigning such individuals stage 1A; they dispute treating this finding alone as a clinical disease diagnosis. (low confidence)

The Braak pathological sequence is not universal across patients or Lewy-body disorders; reviews describe nonconforming distributions, so it should not be assumed to represent every patient’s disease course. (medium confidence)

Burke and colleagues cautioned that Braak pathological stages cannot be directly equated with clinical severity or inevitable future clinical Parkinson’s disease: their review describes advanced pathological stages in neurologically unimpaired individuals and no relationship with clinical severity in the data examined. (low confidence)

SynNeurGe’s proposed biological classification has three components: pathological α-synuclein in tissues or CSF (S), imaging evidence of neurodegeneration (N), and pathogenic variants that cause or strongly predispose to Parkinson’s disease (G). (medium confidence)

Published interpretations differ: an autopsy-based study concluded that the PD staging scheme is valid except in the setting of advanced Alzheimer’s disease, whereas Burke and colleagues judged the evidence insufficient to establish the proposed caudal-to-rostral temporal progression of human Parkinson’s disease. (low confidence)

In an analysis of PPMI, PASADENA and SPARK data published in npj Parkinson's Disease in 2024, 1741 participants had SAA data and 1030 (59%) were S+ consistent with neuronal alpha-synuclein disease (NSD); among sporadic PD, 683/736 (93%) were NSD, with a baseline distribution across NSD-ISS Stages 2B, 3 and 4 of 25%, 63% and 9%. The authors state that validation of the proposed anchors in longitudinal cohorts is necessary. (low confidence)

Isolated RBD involves dream enactment and loss of normal REM sleep atonia in the absence of an established neurodegenerative disorder. The cited risk cohorts used polysomnography-confirmed RBD; their estimates should not be assigned to questionnaire-positive dream enactment alone. (high confidence)

Isolated RBD is a strong prodromal marker for a spectrum of neurodegenerative outcomes, including Parkinson’s disease, dementia with Lewy bodies and multiple system atrophy; a reported overall phenoconversion rate is therefore not a PD-only conversion rate. (medium confidence)

A 2019 meta-analysis of seven prospective studies reported an association between hyposmia and subsequent PD, with pooled relative risk 3.84 (95% CI 2.12–6.95) across follow-up periods of 3–17 years. This relative risk is not an absolute probability that a person with hyposmia will develop PD. (low confidence)

RBD conversion estimates depend on population, age, endpoint definitions and ascertainment. The 2019 multicentre investigators warned that predictor hazard ratios should not be extrapolated to the general population, and the 2024 Mayo investigators called for population-based, polysomnography-confirmed cohorts to quantify community risk. (medium confidence)

A negative baseline prodromal assessment cannot reliably rule out later phenoconversion in iRBD. In the 2019 cohort, even participants negative for the MDS prodromal criteria had conversion estimates of 5% at 3 years, 13% at 5 years and 27% at 8 years. (low confidence)

In the 2023 cross-sectional PPMI study, CSF SAA sensitivity for clinically diagnosed Parkinson disease was 87·7% (95% CI 84·9–90·5) and specificity against healthy controls was 96·3% (93·4–99·2); these estimates describe that study population rather than general-population screening. (low confidence)

SAA positivity is heterogeneous: in the 2023 PPMI study, sensitivity in sporadic Parkinson disease with olfactory deficit was 98·6%, compared with 78·3% without olfactory deficit. A negative result therefore cannot universally exclude clinically diagnosed Parkinson disease. (low confidence)
NfL is a marker of neuroaxonal injury that can complement alpha-synuclein SAA, rather than directly measuring alpha-synuclein seeds. (low confidence)

In the 2025 head-to-head NfL study, CSF assays discriminated Parkinson’s disease from atypical parkinsonian disorders more accurately than plasma assays (AUC 0.966–0.974 versus 0.917–0.924); combining CSF NfL with alpha-synuclein RT-QuIC improved accuracy in that cohort. (low confidence)

The 2024 Zarkali review reports associations of baseline CSF Alzheimer-related biomarkers—higher phosphorylated tau, lower amyloid-beta 42, and lower amyloid-beta 42/total tau ratio—with worsening motor and cognitive performance at follow-up; these characterize co-pathology and prognosis rather than alpha-synuclein seeding itself. (low confidence)

In a blinded 30-site cross-sectional study, skin biopsy detected cutaneous phosphorylated alpha-synuclein in 92.7% (89 of 96) of patients with PD, 98.2% (54 of 55) with MSA, 96.0% (48 of 50) with DLB and 100% (22 of 22) with pure autonomic failure, versus 3.3% (4 of 120) of controls; the authors state that further research in unselected clinical populations is needed to externally validate the findings. (low confidence)

The Camp Lejeune cohort study found higher odds of PD among veterans stationed at the contaminated base than among Camp Pendleton veterans (OR 1.70, 95% CI 1.39–2.07). Exposure concerned water containing TCE and other volatile organic compounds, rather than an isolated TCE exposure. (low confidence)

The critical review by Atterling Brolin and colleagues argues that converging epidemiological and experimental evidence supports stronger environmental policy action; this is the review authors’ assessment of causality and prevention, rather than proof that every exposure causes PD. (low confidence)

A UK paraquat-manufacturing workforce mortality study found no evidence of increased PD mortality (SMR 0.67, 95% CI 0.18–1.72). It assessed death-certificate outcomes rather than incident PD and disclosed Syngenta funding. (low confidence)

In the Global Burden of Disease analysis, 6·1 million (95% uncertainty interval 5·0-7·3) individuals had Parkinson's disease globally in 2016, compared with 2·5 million (2·0-3·0) in 1990; age-standardised prevalence rates increased by 21·7% (95% UI 18·1-25·3) over the same period. (low confidence)

In the 2025 UK Biobank/LuxPark study, severe and mild GBA1 variant groups had nearly double the PD risk of the risk-variant group, and polygenic background further stratified risk. These are cohort associations rather than a deterministic individual prediction. (low confidence)

In the EANM/SNMMI guideline, early idiopathic Parkinson’s disease typically shows reduced uptake first in the posterior putamen opposite the symptomatic side, with greater putaminal than caudate involvement; this is a typical pattern rather than a disease-specific signature. (low confidence)

The EANM/SNMMI guideline interprets persistent scans without dopaminergic deficit as evidence against idiopathic PD; Palermo and colleagues instead reported eight older-onset levodopa-responsive cases with initially normal scans, two later abnormal. Their cases lacked pathological confirmation, so this is an attributed limitation rather than proof that normal scans commonly miss PD. (medium confidence)

A 2023 retrospective clinical series of 156 patients referred for suspected atypical parkinsonism found overall FDG-PET classification accuracy of 74%, using follow-up clinical diagnosis rather than autopsy as the reference; the reader had access to prior dopamine-transporter imaging. The authors acknowledge reference-standard bias and missing histopathological confirmation. (low confidence)

DaTscan uses iodine-123 ioflupane SPECT to visualize striatal dopamine transporter availability; it is an adjunct to other diagnostic evaluations rather than a standalone disease identification test. (medium confidence)

For dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB), the DATSCAN label reports, in 55 patients clinically diagnosed with DLB or Alzheimer's disease and compared with autopsy diagnosis, sensitivity of 80% (95% CI 61% to 92%) and specificity of 92% (95% CI 74% to 99%); the label derives this evidence from the scientific literature. (low confidence)

A meta-analysis of nigrosome-1 appearance on MRI included nineteen studies with a total of 1508 participants (903 idiopathic PD patients and 605 healthy controls) and reported pooled sensitivity 0.94 (95 percent CI 0.93-0.96) and specificity 0.90 (95 percent CI 0.88-0.92) for differentiating idiopathic PD from healthy adults; the comparison was with healthy adults rather than other parkinsonian syndromes. (low confidence)
Asymmetric parkinsonism with higher cortical features such as apraxia, cortical sensory loss or alien-limb phenomena suggests corticobasal syndrome rather than typical PD. (low confidence)

Braak staging proposes a neuropathological sequence beginning in lower-brainstem or olfactory structures, proceeding toward substantia nigra involvement and eventually cortex; the proposed direction of spread is a hypothesis rather than a clinical disability score. (medium confidence)

Braak’s six-pattern scheme inferred temporal progression from progressively broader postmortem distributions of abnormal α-synuclein staining; in that proposed sequence substantia-nigra involvement appears around stage 3, rather than at its earliest stage. (low confidence)

The MDS research framework combines an age-based prior probability with marker likelihood ratios in a Bayesian naïve classifier; probable prodromal PD means at least 80% estimated certainty that prodromal disease is present, rather than an 80% prediction of clinical conversion within a specified number of years. (high confidence)

Postuma and colleagues’ 2019 study followed 1280 polysomnography-confirmed iRBD patients from 24 centres: mean age was 66.3 years, 82.5% were men, and mean follow-up was 4.6 years. Overall conversion to an overt neurodegenerative syndrome was 6.3% per year, with Kaplan–Meier estimated conversion of 73.5% at 12 years; these are study estimates rather than universal individual prognoses. (low confidence)

The 2024 Lifelines analysis found poor discrimination (ROC-AUC 0.577) using a subset of MDS risk and prodromal markers in 160 self-reported PD converters and 320 matched controls. Only six of eleven risk markers and six of twelve prodromal markers could be inferred, so this result scopes a partial, largely questionnaire-based implementation rather than invalidating the complete criteria. (low confidence)

Alpha-synuclein SAA detects seeding-competent misfolded aggregates by amplifying their ability to template recombinant alpha-synuclein aggregation; thioflavin T fluorescence detects the resulting fibrils. RT-QuIC and PMCA are related SAA approaches. (high confidence)

Expert-laboratory concordance does not remove the need for assay standardization: protocol heterogeneity, recombinant substrate, buffers, beads, shaking, temperature, and preanalytical handling affect comparability. (high confidence)

Blood alpha-synuclein assays require control of peripheral contamination and sample handling: erythrocytes and platelets contribute alpha-synuclein, and hemolysis and storage conditions can vary results. CSF SAA also requires preanalytical controls, including blood contamination and freeze-thaw handling. (high confidence)

SAA seeding activity and total CSF alpha-synuclein concentration are different measurements: the 2024 Zarkali review found that total CSF alpha-synuclein did not show a consistent relationship with Lewy body pathology or longitudinal motor or cognitive change. (low confidence)

Longitudinal prognostic results differ by analysis: a PPMI analysis found no statistically significant association between baseline seeding measures and progression among manifest patients, whereas a separate analysis associated baseline time-to-threshold with subsequent cognitive decline in PPMI and an independent Tübingen cohort. Diagnostic positivity should not be treated as an established general progression measure. (medium confidence)

CSF sampling is relatively invasive, motivating SAA studies in other specimens. The 2024 Zarkali review describes promising skin-biopsy results and lower accuracy with olfactory-mucosa sampling; performance should be interpreted for the specimen and assay actually tested. (low confidence)
Goldman and colleagues’ discordant-twin study associated TCE exposure with PD (OR 6.1, 95 percent CI 1.2–33). The very wide interval makes the effect size imprecise. (low confidence)

Xie and colleagues’ 2025 meta-analysis estimated a pooled OR of 1.10 (95 percent CI 1.03–1.17) for PD with each 5 μg/m3 increase in long-term PM2.5 exposure. This is an observational pooled association. (low confidence)

The 2025 Northern Ireland cohort found no adjusted overall association between medium-term PM₂.₅ or NO2 exposure and medication-defined PD onset, but reported a positive PM₂.₅ association in participants under 50. Its findings therefore do not support a uniform association across age groups. (low confidence)

A nationwide Taiwan cohort reported positive associations between air-pollutant exposure and PD incidence that persisted in multipollutant models; this observational result does not establish a universal exposure effect. (low confidence)
In the same projection, population ageing was the largest contributor to the projected growth in cases, ahead of population growth and changes in prevalence. (low confidence)

Heterozygous GBA1 variants increase PD susceptibility with variable penetrance influenced by age, variant and genetic background; a carrier result alone does not establish that PD will develop. (medium confidence)

PD panels need attention to copy-number analysis: sequencing alone may miss deletions or duplications, particularly relevant to SNCA and PRKN. Check whether the assay includes deletion/duplication testing. (medium confidence)

GBA1 coverage differs among laboratories: verify inclusion and full sequencing. Expanded testing can identify variants of uncertain significance that require expert interpretation and may remain inconclusive. (low confidence)

Genetic counseling should explain inheritance, penetrance and test limitations. Expert review supports pretest and posttest counseling; GeneReviews specifically recommends discussing limitations and consequences before predictive testing of asymptomatic relatives. (medium confidence)
Testing beyond selected known variants can reveal variants of uncertain significance requiring expert interpretation; such findings may not establish pathogenicity. (low confidence)

DAT-SPECT interpretation requires checking potentially interfering drugs and structural imaging: cocaine, amphetamines and methylphenidate can markedly reduce tracer binding, while anatomic lesions and atrophy can alter apparent striatal binding or shape. Medication changes require clinician-directed preparation. (low confidence)

A 2014 primary MRI study showed that healthy nigrosome-1 can appear as a swallow-tail hyperintensity on high-resolution 3T susceptibility-weighted imaging, with this appearance lost in PD. The authors called for independent prospective validation. (low confidence)

The 2024 7T MRI authors identify small sample size, retrospective design and inclusion of established PD as limitations, and call for studies in equivocal PD and atypical parkinsonism; their reported accuracy should not be assumed to generalize to routine diagnostic populations. (low confidence)

In the same 7T study, neuromelanin volume discriminated groups, whereas contrast ratio did not differ significantly between PD and non-PD groups; a result for one MRI metric should not be generalized to all neuromelanin measurements. (low confidence)

In a retrospective study of eighty-three clinically confirmed degenerative parkinsonian cases, voxel-based FDG-PET maps added diagnostic accuracy and confidence, particularly for less experienced readers; expert-reader improvement was mainly supported by hypometabolism maps. (low confidence)

DAT-SPECT quantification requires attention to acquisition and processing: the EANM/SNMMI guideline cautions that specific binding ratios from different cameras, acquisition methods, processing and analyses are not directly interchangeable. (low confidence)

The FDA prescribing information for DATSCAN (ioflupane I 123 injection), revised 11/2022, indicates it as an adjunct to other diagnostic evaluations for striatal dopamine transporter visualization using single photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) brain imaging in adult patients with suspected parkinsonian syndromes or suspected dementia with Lewy bodies. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27)
MDS bradykinesia requires slowness plus decrement in amplitude or speed, or progressive hesitations/halts, during continued movement; limb bradykinesia must be documented. (low confidence)

Clinically established PD under the 2015 MDS criteria requires no absolute exclusion, at least two supportive criteria, and no red flags. Clinically probable PD permits at most two red flags, each counterbalanced by a supportive criterion, with no absolute exclusion. (medium confidence)

Supportive MDS features include a clear and dramatic dopaminergic treatment response, levodopa-induced dyskinesia, and clinically documented limb rest tremor; merely some improvement on treatment does not satisfy the dramatic-response criterion. (low confidence)

Examples of 2015 MDS absolute exclusions are unequivocal cerebellar abnormalities, downward vertical supranuclear gaze palsy or selective slowing of downward saccades, and dopamine-blocking/depleting exposure whose dose and time course fit drug-induced parkinsonism. (low confidence)
Essential tremor commonly produces bilateral postural/action tremor; PD can also have postural/action tremor, so tremor appearance alone is insufficient for diagnosis. (low confidence)

Medication review is central to differential diagnosis: drug-induced parkinsonism can be symmetric but can also closely mimic PD; symptoms often resolve after withdrawal, while continued progression can reflect underlying PD unmasked by the drug. (low confidence)

Early prominent autonomic problems, cerebellar signs or stridor raise suspicion of multiple system atrophy; early falls with vertical eye-movement abnormalities raise suspicion of progressive supranuclear palsy. These are differential clues, not guarantees of pathology. (medium confidence)

Functional parkinsonism is assessed using positive examination signs such as effortful slowness without decrement, improvement with distraction, variable tremor, and active resistance during passive movement. (low confidence)

The autopsy-based scoping review by Fox and colleagues found that supportive features were more common in PD and exclusions/red flags more common in atypical disorders, but some atypical features also occurred in pathologically confirmed PD. Limited clinical documentation, retrospective application of precise definitions and co-pathology constrain interpretation. (low confidence)

NICE guideline NG71 (published 19 July 2017) advises against acute levodopa and apomorphine challenge tests in the differential diagnosis of parkinsonian syndromes, and against objective smell testing in that setting except in the context of clinical trials. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27)
Hoehn–Yahr stage 1 describes unilateral involvement; stage 2 describes bilateral or midline involvement without impaired balance. (medium confidence)
Hoehn–Yahr stage three is marked by impaired balance and mild-to-moderate disability, while the person remains physically capable of independent living. (medium confidence)
Hoehn–Yahr stage 4 denotes severe disability with standing or walking still possible unassisted; stage 5 denotes confinement to a bed or wheelchair unless aided. (medium confidence)

SynNeurGe classifies pathological α-synuclein (S), neurodegeneration (N), and pathogenic genetic variants (G), linked to clinical manifestations (C); these are biological classification dimensions. (medium confidence)
The 2024 SynNeurGe proposal specifies initial use exclusively for research and acknowledges ethical implications, limitations and the need for prospective validation. (medium confidence)

Braak and colleagues interpreted increasingly extensive, nested pathological distributions as a temporal sequence: stage 1 involved medulla or olfactory structures, stage 2 added rostrally adjacent brainstem structures, and stages 3–4 were proposed to coincide with substantia nigra neuron loss and clinical parkinsonism. (low confidence)

Prodromal PD describes early symptoms or signs of neurodegeneration before fully evolved motor parkinsonism permits a classic clinical diagnosis; the original MDS prodromal criteria were explicitly developed for research purposes only. (high confidence)

In the same 2019 iRBD cohort, olfactory deficit predicted faster phenoconversion (adjusted hazard ratio 2.62), alongside quantitative motor abnormalities (3.16) and mild cognitive impairment (1.91–2.37); the outcome was overall neurodegenerative phenoconversion. (low confidence)

Smell loss alone has limited specificity: it can occur in neurological diseases other than PD. The hyposmia meta-analysis explicitly cautioned that the limited evidence did not establish hyposmia as a solid stand-alone predictor of PD. (medium confidence)

The 2019 update of the MDS prodromal framework revised marker weights using new prospective evidence; in particular, the positive likelihood ratio for olfactory loss increased, while many marker likelihood ratios were unchanged. (low confidence)

narrative.documentConcept: Alpha-synuclein seed amplification assay and fluid biomarkers
narrative.text: Alpha-synuclein seed amplification assays amplify seeding-competent aggregates and provide a molecular biomarker of synuclein pathology. CSF studies show strong diagnostic performance in selected cohorts, with clinically important heterogeneity in sensitivity. Cross-laboratory results are encouraging, but protocol and preanalytical standardization remain necessary. Diagnostic positivity is distinct from validated measurement of severity or progression. Blood assays offer less invasive sampling while introducing contamination and handling challenges. Neurofilament light chain measures neuroaxonal injury and can complement SAA, with interpretation influenced by biological covariates. FDA support described here concerns trial enrichment in its 2024 letter. Skin biopsy detection of phosphorylated alpha-synuclein is another tissue biomarker under evaluation.

narrative.documentConcept: Alpha-synuclein seed amplification assay and fluid biomarkers
narrative.text: One PPMI analysis reported no significant baseline SAA–progression association among manifest patients; a separate analysis reported cognitive-decline associations for time-to-threshold in PPMI and Tübingen cohorts. The analyses differ in method and outcome, so they are not replications of the same endpoint.

narrative.documentConcept: Clinical rating scales and outcome measures: MDS-UPDRS
narrative.text: MDS-UPDRS measures non-motor and motor daily-life experiences, motor examination findings, and motor complications in Parkinson’s disease. Validation supports use of its separate parts, while clinically meaningful change estimates depend on the part and direction of change. Repeated motor examinations require attention to medication and ON/OFF state. Longitudinal reliability and early-disease floor effects limit interpretation of small changes in individuals. Original UPDRS scores require calibration rather than direct substitution. Complementary instruments include the MDS Non-Motor Rating Scale and the PDQ-39 quality-of-life questionnaire.

narrative.text: How well do the cited MCID estimates generalize to specific trial populations and medication states?

narrative.documentConcept: Clinical rating scales and outcome measures: MDS-UPDRS
narrative.text: Several primary studies were available here through PubMed abstracts rather than full article bodies; evidence pins attest only to the retrieved abstract passages.

narrative.documentConcept: Epidemiology and environmental risk factors: paraquat, TCE, air pollution
narrative.text: PD epidemiology includes a rising global burden (Global Burden of Disease estimates and projections) and potentially modifiable environmental exposures. Observational studies associate paraquat, TCE-containing solvent exposures and some air pollutants with PD, but estimates and causal interpretations vary. Paraquat findings include positive case-control results, null workforce mortality evidence and a qualified EPA assessment finding no clear link for labeled uses. TCE evidence includes a small twin study and the mixed-exposure Camp Lejeune cohort. Air-pollution evidence includes positive pooled and Taiwanese results alongside an adjusted overall null Northern Ireland result. Forecasts, odds ratios, exposure mixtures and study outcomes require separate interpretation.

narrative.documentConcept: Epidemiology and environmental risk factors: paraquat, TCE, air pollution
narrative.text: Tanner et al. reported increased PD odds with paraquat; EPA states that it has not found a clear link for labeled uses. A paraquat systematic review and meta-analysis described a positive association without an indisputable causal conclusion.

narrative.documentConcept: Epidemiology and environmental risk factors: paraquat, TCE, air pollution
narrative.text: The air-pollution meta-analysis and Taiwanese cohort report positive associations, whereas Northern Ireland reports an adjusted overall null association with a younger-subgroup exception; exposure duration, population and outcome definitions differ.

narrative.documentConcept: Epidemiology and environmental risk factors: paraquat, TCE, air pollution
narrative.text: FAME reported higher PD odds with paraquat use; the later prospective AHS analysis did not show a statistically clear association. Both draw on the Agricultural Health Study and are not independent cohorts.

narrative.text: Which exposure windows and doses explain the heterogeneous PD associations across studies?

narrative.documentConcept: Genetics of PD: LRRK2, GBA1, SNCA, PRKN, PINK1
narrative.text: PD genetics spans dominant LRRK2 and SNCA disease, recessive PRKN and PINK1 disease, and variably penetrant GBA1-associated susceptibility. Variant identity, age, ancestry and ascertainment affect interpretation. Genetic testing can identify trial-relevant subgroups, but reportable variants are not synonymous with confirmed monogenic diagnoses. Reliable interpretation requires appropriate copy-number and GBA1 coverage, distinction between monoallelic and biallelic findings, and genetic counseling. Cohort-specific penetrance estimates should not be treated as deterministic predictions for an individual. Genome-wide association studies add common-variant risk loci beyond the monogenic genes.

narrative.documentConcept: Genetics of PD: LRRK2, GBA1, SNCA, PRKN, PINK1
narrative.text: GeneReviews reports disagreement over classifying GBA1-associated PD as monogenic disease versus a risk-factor association because penetrance is low, particularly in population cohorts. GeneReviews notes that some Gaucher-causing GBA1 variants have PD penetrance approaching LRRK2 pathogenic variants.

narrative.documentConcept: Genetics of PD: LRRK2, GBA1, SNCA, PRKN, PINK1
narrative.text: What prospective, ancestry-diverse estimates would best calibrate individual carrier risk across variant classes?

narrative.documentConcept: Imaging biomarkers: DaTscan, MRI and PET
narrative.text: Imaging contributes complementary evidence rather than a single disease-specific answer. Dopamine-transporter SPECT identifies presynaptic dysfunction but does not reliably separate PD from atypical degenerative parkinsonism. Structural MRI helps assess alternative causes; nigrosome and neuromelanin MRI offer promising research measures whose diagnostic performance depends on population, acquisition and validation. FDG-PET examines cerebral metabolic patterns, whereas fluorodopa PET assesses presynaptic dopaminergic function. Small MRI case-control studies should not be equated with routine clinical accuracy. Drug interference, structural lesions, non-diagnostic scans and clinical rather than pathological reference standards constrain interpretation. Selected older-onset cases with initially normal DAT-SPECT further caution against absolute exclusion claims. The FDA label positions DaTscan as an adjunct to other diagnostic evaluations, and NICE NG71 recommends considering it when essential tremor cannot be clinically differentiated from parkinsonism.

narrative.documentConcept: Imaging biomarkers: DaTscan, MRI and PET
narrative.text: EANM/SNMMI regards persistent SWEDD as unlikely idiopathic PD; Palermo et al. describe selected older-onset clinical cases with initially normal imaging and argue for possible false negatives, while acknowledging absent pathological confirmation. This is a difference in scope and interpretation, not an established general false-negative rate.

narrative.documentConcept: PD diagnosis criteria and differential diagnosis
narrative.text: PD diagnosis requires distinguishing motor parkinsonism from its cause. The 2015 MDS criteria combine a mandatory motor syndrome with absolute exclusions, supportive findings and timed red flags, with separate clinically established and clinically probable categories. Specialist history, examination, medication review and reassessment help distinguish PD from essential tremor, drug-induced and vascular parkinsonism, normal-pressure hydrocephalus, functional presentations and atypical neurodegenerative syndromes. Published validation against expert diagnosis should be distinguished from pathological confirmation; autopsy series show clinical overlap and limitations of retrospective documentation.

narrative.documentConcept: PD staging: Hoehn-Yahr, Braak and biological SynNeurGe
narrative.text: Hoehn–Yahr describes motor disability, especially laterality, balance and physical independence. Braak staging describes a proposed sequence of postmortem α-synuclein pathology; exceptions limit its interpretation as a universal course or clinical severity measure. SynNeurGe combines synuclein pathology, neurodegeneration and genetics with clinical manifestations for research classification. Its authors explicitly refrained from proposing a temporal staging sequence, distinguishing it from NSD-ISS. These frameworks answer different questions and should be identified by name when comparing research populations. The NSD-ISS has been applied to PPMI, PASADENA and SPARK data.

narrative.documentConcept: PD staging: Hoehn-Yahr, Braak and biological SynNeurGe
narrative.text: The Braak model proposes ordered spread from lower-brainstem/olfactory structures; Burke and colleagues question its predictive universality, while Rietdijk and colleagues find supportive evidence but restrict staging fit to a subset. These are attributed interpretations, not proof of a universal sequence.

narrative.documentConcept: PD staging: Hoehn-Yahr, Braak and biological SynNeurGe
narrative.text: One autopsy-based study supported Braak staging with an advanced-Alzheimer-pathology exception; Burke et al. questioned whether the observed anatomical patterns establish temporal progression. These are attributed interpretations with different emphasis, not proof that all patients follow a single sequence.

narrative.documentConcept: PD staging: Hoehn-Yahr, Braak and biological SynNeurGe
narrative.text: What prospective evidence would establish a reproducible temporal ordering of SynNeurGe categories across heterogeneous PD populations?

narrative.documentConcept: PD staging: Hoehn-Yahr, Braak and biological SynNeurGe
narrative.text: What prospective longitudinal validation would justify mapping SynNeurGe biological categories to sequential stages?

narrative.documentConcept: Prodromal PD: RBD, hyposmia and risk prediction
narrative.text: Prodromal PD research estimates disease probability before classic motor diagnosis by combining age and risk-marker information. Polysomnography-confirmed isolated REM sleep behaviour disorder is a strong marker, but its phenoconversion outcomes include dementia and other disorders as well as PD. Hyposmia is associated with increased subsequent PD risk yet has limited specificity. Cohort conversion percentages, relative risks and Bayesian prodromal probabilities describe different quantities and should not be substituted for an individual forecast. The MDS research framework and its 2019 update support research stratification; the 2019 multicentre RBD study, 2024 Mayo cohort and 2024 Lifelines analysis demonstrate why population, ascertainment, marker availability and follow-up matter.

narrative.documentConcept: Prodromal PD: RBD, hyposmia and risk prediction
narrative.text: How should prospective community cohorts calibrate individual time-to-PD prediction separately from conversion to other neurodegenerative endpoints?
